summary:
GO / NO-GO is an interactive space mission design and simulation game that allows players to experience the complete process of planning, launching, and operating a space mission. Players define mission objectives, design spacecraft, select or build rockets, manage mass, power, budget, communications, and fuel, and then simulate launches using real physics equations.

The game features NASA-inspired missions including Landsat 9, Hubble, and Apollo 11, alongside a wildfire-monitoring mission using real NASA FIRMS active fire data. Players can operate spacecraft in orbit, photograph real wildfire locations, communicate with ground stations, avoid space debris, and analyse mission outcomes.

With guided and manual flight modes, a four-role cooperative team mode, a custom rocket builder, sandbox missions, and a built-in Physics Lab, GO / NO-GO makes complex space engineering concepts interactive and accessible to everyone. Its goal is to make space mission design and scientific problem-solving engaging through hands-on experimentation.
details:
GO / NO-GO is an interactive 2D space mission design and simulation game developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 under the challenge "Space Mission Design Game."

What does it do and how does it work?

The game allows players to experience the complete lifecycle of a space mission, from defining its objective and designing a spacecraft to building a launch vehicle, executing a launch, operating the spacecraft in orbit, and evaluating mission performance.

Players can choose from different missions, including Wildfire Watcher, Landsat 9, Hubble, and Apollo 11, or create their own objectives through Sandbox mode.

The spacecraft design system allows players to select scientific instruments, solar panels, batteries, antennas, and thruster fuel. Six live engineering gauges evaluate mass, power, budget, data, communications, and mission lifetime.

Players can select existing rockets or construct custom launch vehicles using a drag-and-drop rocket builder. Before launch, the game performs a pre-flight simulation and provides a GO or NO-GO decision based on whether the design can achieve its target orbit.

Scientific and technical implementation

The simulation implements real physics concepts and equations, including Newtonian gravitational acceleration, the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, atmospheric drag, variable engine performance, orbital mechanics, Kepler's equations, vis-viva, and fourth-order Runge-Kutta numerical integration.

The game also models atmospheric pressure, Mach number, dynamic pressure, staging, orbital insertion, circularization, eclipses, solar power generation, communication windows, and debris avoidance.

Apollo 11 provides an additional lunar mission experience, including translunar injection, lunar orbit insertion, and a simplified powered lunar descent.

NASA data integration

The project uses NASA FIRMS active fire observations to provide real wildfire locations for spacecraft observation and orbital coverage calculations. NASA Blue Marble and Black Marble imagery provide Earth's surface and night-time city lights. NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter imagery provides the Moon's surface.

Real NASA mission information and reference data are incorporated into the Landsat 9, Hubble, and Apollo 11 scenarios. NASA Near Space Network ground-station information is used to model spacecraft communication opportunities.

Innovation and educational impact

The project combines mission planning, engineering trade-offs, scientific simulation, and interactive gameplay in one experience.

Its four-player cooperative mode introduces Scientist, Engineer, Communications Lead, and Program Manager roles. Each role has different objectives, encouraging collaboration and negotiation through a pre-launch Go/No-Go poll and in-flight mission-control tasks.

The Physics Lab provides 17 validation checks against known scientific reference values. The mission scoring system explains the consequences of engineering decisions, while failure replays help players understand why a mission failed.

Technology used

The game was developed using HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript ES modules, Canvas rendering, and SVG-based rocket diagrams. Python is used for the local development server and NASA FIRMS data-fetching script. Node.js is used for automated testing.

The game has no external runtime dependencies or framework requirements. Its NASA imagery and datasets are packaged locally, allowing the downloaded game to run without an internet connection.

GO / NO-GO aims to make space engineering more understandable and accessible by allowing people to experiment, make decisions, encounter realistic engineering constraints, and learn from the outcomes of their own space missions.

  1. Claude Code (Anthropic) – AI-assisted software development tool used for code generation, feature implementation, debugging, troubleshooting and testing.
  2. Python – Used for the local development server and NASA FIRMS data-fetching script.
  3. Node.js – Used for executing automated project tests.
  4. MDN Web Docs – Technical documentation and reference material for HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript ES modules and Canvas API.

AI Assistance Disclosure:

Claude Code, an AI-assisted software development tool, was used during the development of GO / NO-GO to assist with code generation, implementation, debugging, troubleshooting, and automated testing. The development process involved iterative human direction, feature decisions, testing, and refinement.

All NASA datasets and scientific reference materials used in the project are identified in the NASA Data and Resources section.
